general.temas: The November 29 election campaign dominates the front pages, with particular attention to Feijóo’s rally in Madrid. Protests against gender-based violence, Puigdemont’s announced return, new US tariffs and Barça’s victory also feature repeatedly. Público has an exclusive on digital gender-based violence and the role of platforms.
general.motivo_crispacion: The election campaign is a focus of attacks between parties, with Feijóo and Ayuso making accusations against the government and the PSOE. Gender-based violence has brought thousands of women onto the streets and is linked to the election debate, with criticism of the PP and Vox and fears of setbacks. Puigdemont’s announced return and new US tariffs add to political and international tensions. Sports news, recipes and measures for the self-employed provide a calmer counterpoint.

El País.resumen:
- The November 29 campaign dominates the front page, with polls, analysis of tactical voting, interviews and a comparison tool for party manifestos.
- The four candidates prepare for the final major debate; Feijóo appeals to former Socialist voters, and Sánchez promises to increase the pension reserve fund.
- The November 25 demonstrations bring together tens of thousands of women against gender-based violence.
- Puigdemont announces his return to Barcelona on December 12, while a proponent of “remigration” presents a deportation plan.
- The paper reports the release of 11 sex trafficking victims and long queues to vote by post.
El País.motivo_populismo: Election coverage predominates, although expressions such as “endless queues” and “they forced them into prostitution 24 hours a day” add intensity; forceful statements by those involved are also reported.
El País.sesgo: The front page gives particular attention to the election campaign and tactical voting, with a critical approach to the PP and Vox in stories about immigration and postal voting. It also highlights the feminist mobilisation and reports criticism of the government and the PSOE.

El Mundo.resumen:
- Feijóo appeals for votes alongside Ayuso and Almeida; the front page also offers an election questionnaire and reports expressions of support for the Broad Front.
- Puigdemont announces his return to Spain following the amnesty.
- A housing story reflects the precarious situation of tenants; the government announces a tax cut for the self-employed.
- Germany raises the alarm about Russia, the US announces tariffs and Clavijo calls for help with the migration emergency on El Hierro.
- Veterinary courses will be extended to six years; Barça’s emphatic win and the situation of Etxalar’s pigeon hunters also feature prominently.
El Mundo.motivo_populismo: Although informative headlines are plentiful, confrontational quotes such as “tear down the wall” and “get criminals off the streets and out of the government” stand out, alongside alarming expressions such as “SOS” and “emergency”.
El Mundo.sesgo: The front page prioritises the election campaign and confrontational political statements, although it includes voices from different parties. In the story about Puigdemont, the description of him as a “fugitive from justice” adds a critical slant.

ABC.resumen:
- Feijóo promises to bring “decency” back to government and is the subject of two stories about his campaign.
- Sánchez takes part in a conversation and a bike ride with Plex.
- Trump proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU.
- The front page carries stories about Barça, Real Madrid and a goal by Julián.
- It also includes recipes, cooking tips and the headline “Coats made from the skin of the self-employed”.
ABC.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “bring back decency”, “tear down Sánchez’s wall” and “trade war” add confrontation and intensity, although informative and everyday headlines are plentiful.
ABC.sesgo: The selection devotes two stories to Feijóo, focusing on his promises and his rapport with people during the campaign, while presenting Sánchez in a relaxed setting. The front page combines politics with sport and lifestyle content.

Público.resumen:
- Digital gender-based violence and the responsibility of platforms are the focus of several stories.
- The Civil Guard is investigating the murder of a woman in Murcia as a gender-based crime.
- The November 25 protests and equality are linked to the upcoming election.
- The government strengthens abortion safeguards and extends parental leave.
- A judge summons Leire Díez and the former president of Correos as suspects following a criminal complaint by Vox.
Público.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “impunity” and “denialism”, the question “How many women must be murdered before it seems like too many?” and the reference to “The Handmaid’s Tale” add emotional weight and confrontation, although appeals to the people against the elites do not predominate.
Público.sesgo: The front page takes a feminist approach, focusing on violence against women and the rights of women and LGBTI people. It presents the government’s measures favourably and criticises the PP and Vox for their stance on gender-based violence.

OKdiario.resumen:
- The police pay tribute to the dog Deny and his handler, who died in Oviedo.
- Ferran Adrià recalls the financial difficulties he experienced despite his professional success.
- Barcelona thrash Sabah with contributions from less frequently used players.
- Ayuso and Feijóo criticise the PSOE and the government at a campaign event.
- The front page includes stories about television, well-known figures, housing and octopus catches in the United Kingdom.
OKdiario.motivo_populismo: The political disparagement in the quotes from Ayuso and Feijóo, the presentation of Ayuso as someone who “exposes” the PSOE, and eye-catching expressions such as “rebels” and “octopus plague” stand out.
OKdiario.sesgo: The political stories give space to messages critical of the PSOE and the government from PP leaders; the verb “exposing” presents Ayuso’s attack favourably. Overall, there is also a preference for personal statements and eye-catching headlines.

opiniones.comunista:
Today I see a campaign obsessed with the polls while housing reveals an everyday class struggle: rents are rising faster than wages, and many renters fear they will not be able to find another home. This is not inevitable: housing must stop being a business for big capital. I support expanding public housing and collective ownership, with affordable rents and democratic management.

I also listen to the women filling the streets to protest gender-based violence. Their safety requires adequate public services, protection and economic independence, not just election statements. And I reject deportation plans that seek to divide the working class by origin: in the face of those who make migrants scapegoats, we need rights, a welcome and solidarity.
opiniones.anarquista:
I see the campaign reduced to a calculation of tactical voting while housing becomes unaffordable for renters. I do not trust that changing those in charge will be enough: the state and the parties ask us to delegate precisely the power we need to exercise together. I would rather strengthen tenants’ unions, cooperatives and assemblies capable of defending the right to a home and making decisions without hierarchies.

The November 25 protests remind me that individual freedom requires collective support. In the face of gender-based violence and trafficking, we need support networks, resources and decisions in the hands of those who suffer them, not just election promises. I also reject the deportation plan based on an alleged cultural continuity: no authority should decide who deserves to belong based on their origin. Freedom is not protected by erecting borders, but by organising solidarity among equals.
opiniones.liberal:
I welcome the income tax cut and the simplification of tax returns for the self-employed. People who work for themselves should spend more time serving their clients and less on paperwork. But a free economy needs more than last-minute concessions: moderate taxes, stable rules and a state that spends responsibly.

I am also concerned about the insecurity faced by renters. To ease it, I would rather make construction easier and remove obstacles than trust politicians to set prices without discouraging supply. And I reject the new US tariffs: protecting some producers by making goods more expensive for everyone else is not prosperity, but privilege.

Freedom requires personal responsibility, but also institutions that protect victims of violence and trafficking. A limited state must perform those essential functions well.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see the emergency on El Hierro as the consequence of abandoning effective control of our borders. Spain must help those who arrive, but it must also decide who enters and who stays, combat trafficking networks and carry out returns in accordance with the law. Without borders there is no sovereignty, and without sovereignty election promises are worthless.

Puigdemont’s announced return following the amnesty reminds me of another duty: to defend national unity and equality before the law, without privileges negotiated for political convenience. And in the face of violence against women, I demand effective protection and punishment for the guilty, not a competition of slogans. Our traditions also deserve defending, such as the netting of pigeons in Etxalar: a country that scorns its heritage ends up letting others decide what it should be. I do not expect the political and media elites to admit it.
opiniones.centro:
The November 25 protests remind me that equality is not defended through statements alone: it requires effective protection for victims, stable resources and cooperation between institutions. I also reject the deportation plan based on “ethnocultural continuity”: a democracy must judge people by their actions, not by their origin or a supposed cultural burden.

In the middle of the campaign, I would prefer fewer slogans and more answers to housing insecurity. I believe we need lasting agreements that expand supply, mobilise private investment and strengthen protection for those who cannot afford rent. And in the face of queues for postal voting, the authorities must make it easier to exercise the right to vote and explain the safeguards in place. Democratic debate is not improved by sowing unfounded suspicions, but by offering solutions that can be sustained after the election.
